passages.title: The Fourth Control
paras: In Year 7, my school spent one day each autumn orienteering in a state forest an hour north of the city.
Each pair was given a map, a compass that neither person knew how to use, and a card with twelve numbered squares.
Somewhere in the bush were twelve controls.
You had to find them in order and be back at the car park before the bus left at three.
I was twelve, I had studied the map twice on the bus, and I was certain I would be brilliant at it.
My partner was Imogen, who sat at the back of our maths class and had said perhaps ten words to me all year.
When the maps were handed out, I took ours without asking.
Imogen didn’t argue.
She zipped the compass into her jacket pocket and followed me to the start, where our PE teacher was reading out the rules from a clipboard.
At each control, a metal clipper hung on a string.
You pressed it into the right square on your card, and its teeth left a pattern of tiny holes that no other clipper could make, so nobody could pretend to have been somewhere they hadn’t.
Most controls, the teacher said, were tied at about head height to a tree or a post, though a few were tucked low behind logs or rocks, “where only the patient will find them.”
She called those ones sleepers.
Pairs who couldn’t find one were allowed to move on to the next, but an empty square would cost them.
The first three went perfectly.
I found them so quickly that I began to look at the map less and run more.
Imogen kept up without complaint.
Now and then she glanced at the map over my shoulder, and once she seemed about to say something, but she only pushed her hair behind her ear and kept walking.
I decided she was bored.
She had the look, I thought, of someone counting the minutes until the bus.
The fourth control was meant to be where a creek met a walking track.
When the track split in two, I chose the wider side because it looked more like the line on the map, and for a while I was sure of it.
Then the track began to climb, though the map showed the creek in a gully below us.
I told myself the map was probably out of date.
Soon the track narrowed to a path, the path to a strip of flattened grass, and then it stopped altogether at a wire fence.
Beyond it was a paddock, where three cows watched us with mild interest.
That was when I finally admitted that we were lost.
Imogen took the map from me gently, the way you might take scissors off a small child.
She turned it until the creek on the paper ran the same way as the gully below us, put her thumb on a spot beside the fence and said, “We’re here.”
Then she walked us back down.
Her thumb never left the map; she slid it along as we went, like someone keeping their place in a book.
Within fifteen minutes we were standing beside the creek, and there, tucked under a fallen log, was the fourth control.
She held the map for the rest of the day.
We found every control after that, but we were the last pair back, and the bus had been waiting for twenty minutes.
The PE teacher looked at her watch, then at our card, and wrote something on her clipboard that I couldn’t read.
I spent the ride home sure that we were in trouble.
We weren’t.
The next week our card was pinned to the noticeboard outside the staffroom: the only one in Year 7 with all twelve squares punched.
Most pairs had skipped at least one of the hidden controls so they could make the bus.
It was years before I learnt the rest.

At a friend’s birthday dinner, long after we had all left school, Imogen’s mother told me that Imogen had been orienteering with her family most weekends since she was seven, and that she had come home that day saying the girl she had been partnered with was “fast, but in the wrong direction.”
I have thought about that day more often than I would have expected.
I had taken her silence for boredom, when it was something much closer to patience.
She had let me be wrong until it mattered, and then she had fixed it without once making me feel small.
I still read maps too quickly.
But I have learnt to watch for the person glancing over my shoulder.

passages.title: Inside a Vacuum Flask
paras: Pour hot soup into an ordinary jar on a winter morning, and by lunchtime it will be barely warm.
Pour the same soup into a vacuum flask, and it can still steam when you open it six hours later.
The flask has no battery, no heater and no moving parts.
It keeps soup hot not by adding anything, but by taking something away.
To see how, it helps to know that heat always travels from something warmer to something cooler, and that it can make the trip in three ways.
In conduction, heat passes through a solid from one jiggling particle to the next, which is why the handle of a metal spoon left in a cup of tea soon grows hot.
In convection, a warm liquid or gas rises and carries its heat with it, which is why the air near a ceiling is warmer than the air near the floor.
In radiation, heat leaves a warm object as invisible rays that can cross even empty space, which is how the Sun warms the Earth across millions of kilometres of nothing.
A vacuum flask is built to block all three.
Inside its outer case sits a second container, and the two walls are joined only at the neck.
Before the flask is sealed, almost all the air is pumped out of the narrow gap between them, leaving a vacuum.
With no air in the gap, there are no particles to pass heat along by conduction and no air to rise and carry it away by convection.
Radiation is harder to stop, because it does not need anything to travel through.
So the walls facing the gap are coated with a thin, shiny layer, often silver in older flasks, that works like a mirror.
Heat rays leaving the soup strike the coating and are bounced back toward the drink instead of escaping.
On a hot day the same mirror works in reverse, turning back the warmth of the outside world so that iced water stays cold.
No flask is perfect, though.
Its weakest point is the neck, where the inner and outer walls meet and the stopper sits.
Here there is solid material all the way from the inside to the outside, so a little heat always creeps out by conduction.
Every time the lid comes off, warm air escapes and cooler air rushes in.
That is why most of the heat a flask loses leaves through the top rather than the sides, and why a flask that is opened often cools much faster than one left shut.
The design was not first meant for lunchboxes.
In 1892, the Scottish scientist James Dewar needed to keep liquid gases, so cold that they boil at temperatures far below zero, from warming up and boiling away while he studied them.
His double walled glass vessel, with a vacuum between the walls, held them far longer than any container before it.
Dewar never took out a patent on his design.
In 1904, a German glassblower whose workshop made glass vessels for scientists saw that the same container could keep a drink hot, and his company began selling flasks to ordinary buyers.
Early flasks were fragile.
A sharp knock could crack the thin glass, and once the vacuum was lost, the flask kept a drink warm no better than an ordinary jar.
Explorers and mountain climbers carried them anyway, because a hot drink in freezing conditions mattered more to them than the risk of a broken flask.
Most flasks today have walls of stainless steel instead.
Steel survives being dropped, but it carries heat a little better than glass, so the toughest flasks are not always the ones that stay hot the longest.
The idea has spread far beyond the lunchbox.
Some modern windows have two panes of glass with a vacuum sealed between them, which slows the heat escaping from a room in winter.
Laboratories and hospitals store liquid nitrogen, at nearly 200 degrees below zero, in large vacuum containers that are still called dewars.
More than a century after it was built, the vessel a scientist made to keep gases cold is still doing that job, in almost exactly the way he designed it.

passages.title: Borrow, Don't Buy
paras: In the garage of almost every house on my street, there is a power drill.
I know this because last spring, when I needed to hang a single shelf, I knocked on five doors to borrow one, and all five neighbours had a drill.
Two of them could not remember the last time they had used theirs.
Tomasz, at number 12, still had the price sticker on the box.
That afternoon convinced me of something I now believe strongly: every suburb should have a tool library, run by and for the people who live there.
A tool library works like a book library.
Members pay a small yearly fee, borrow a ladder, a sander or a tent for a week, and then bring it back for the next person.
The first argument is simple arithmetic.
One estimate that is often repeated claims that a typical home drill is used for less than a quarter of an hour in its whole life.
Even if the real figure is 10 times higher, that is a lot of machine sitting in the dark.
Every one of those drills was made, packed, shipped and sold, and most of them spend their lives in a cupboard.
On a street of 40 houses, we are buying 40 drills to do a job that one drill could do for everyone.
The second argument is about space and rubbish.
Garages fill up with things that are used once and then stored for years.
When cheap tools finally break, many of them cannot be repaired, because their parts are glued or riveted together, so they go straight into landfill.
A shared tool, by contrast, is usually a sturdier model that the library can fix, and it is used by dozens of people before it wears out.
The third argument is the one that surprised me.
Two years ago, the suburb next to ours opened a tool library in an empty shop beside the train station, and it has quietly become a meeting place.
Aaliyah, the volunteer who runs the Saturday shift, told me that people often stay to ask how to use what they are borrowing.
Retired tradespeople drop in to show teenagers how to sharpen a chisel or patch a bike tyre.
"Half our members come for a hammer," she said, "and leave knowing something new."
Not everyone is convinced.
Some people worry that borrowed tools will come back broken, or not come back at all, leaving the next borrower with nothing.
Others say the shops that sell tools will lose customers.
A few simply point out that a drill is not expensive, so why bother sharing one?
The library beside the station has answered most of these worries.
It has lost just three tools in two years, partly because every member signs up with an address and every tool is checked when it comes back.
Meanwhile, the library's members still buy their own nails, screws, paint and timber, and many say they now attempt jobs they would once have paid someone else to do.
And while one drill may be cheap, a garage full of tools used once each is not.
Suburbs already share book libraries, swimming pools and playgrounds because some things make more sense shared than owned.
Tools belong on that list.
The cost is small: a shopfront, some shelves, a part time coordinator and a roster of volunteers.
In return, a suburb gets less waste, more space and a place where neighbours meet.
Next time I need a drill, I would rather walk to the station and borrow one from a shelf than knock on five doors again.
I suspect my neighbours would rather that too.
They could keep their garages for the things they actually use, and the whole street could share the rest.

passages.title: A Year at the Lost Property Office
paras: Everything left on a train or bus on the Westbrook network ends up at the same place: a narrow office at the back of Westbrook Central station.
The staff there are often university students working part time, but some are retired drivers who know the network better than anyone.
Owners pay nothing to collect what they have lost, and on a busy Monday the shelves can fill with more than a hundred new things before lunch.
This report looks at the records the office kept over its most recent full year.
In that year, 5,140 items were handed in.
Staff returned 3,090 of them to their owners, which is about three in every five.
Another 410 could not be matched with an owner straight away, usually because there was no name or phone number inside, and their owners were asked to call back once a week.
Most of those owners did call back, but a few never did, and their things are still sitting in a wire cage beside the photocopier.
Umbrellas and wallets were the most common items handed in.
Wallets were the easier of the two to return: of the 312 wallets handed in, 271 went back to their owners, most of them because a card inside carried a name.
Umbrellas were much harder.
Fewer than half of them were ever claimed, often because their owners could not tell them apart from the dozens of other black umbrellas on the shelf.
The few umbrellas that did go home were mostly bright colours, or had something tied to the handle.
School jumpers made up a much smaller share of the items, but they had the highest return rate of any group.
Of the 96 jumpers handed in, all but five found their way home, mostly because two local schools send someone every Friday to collect the whole pile and hand the jumpers back at assembly.
The counter tends to have its longest queue on Monday mornings, partly because only two staff members work there before ten o'clock.
Phones were a different story.
Only a few of the 220 phones handed in were claimed in the first week, mostly those whose lock screen showed an emergency contact.
Some phones can be unlocked by staff with the owner's help over the phone, but staff rarely try it, because a single wrong guess can lock a phone for hours.
The office also compared two ways of reporting a loss.

People who filled in the online lost property form before coming in tended to get their things back more often than people who simply turned up at the counter, and some were matched with their belongings before they even arrived.
Staff think the form may help because it asks people to describe what they lost in detail, but they point out that their records cannot show this for certain.
Items that nobody claims within three months are given to charity shops, but first every bag is emptied and anything with a name in it is checked one last time.
Last year that came to 1.8 tonnes of clothing, bags and umbrellas, about the weight of a large car.
The office says this suggests it is keeping a great deal out of landfill, although staff admit that some of the donated items might still end up in the bin if the shops cannot sell them.
The office will make two changes this year.
It will begin sending text messages to owners whose phone numbers are found inside a bag or wallet, after 140 people asked why nobody had simply called them.
It will also start recording which line each thing was found on, which staff hope will show where things are most often left behind and which stations need a reminder sign by the doors.

passages.title: Wide Open
paras: The trial game started at half past four, and by five o'clock Kenji had looked at the coach's clipboard more often than he had looked at the hoop.
Twelve players had been invited, and only two would make the regional squad.
One of the two had to be a guard, and the only guards on the court were Kenji and Omari.
Kenji had been getting ready since January, shooting at the hoop above the garage every morning before school.
For the first few weeks his mum had knocked on the kitchen window at quarter past eight and pointed at the clock, and he had sprinted for the bus with his laces undone.
Sometime in March the knocking stopped.
After that, his school bag was waiting by the front door each morning, already packed, with his lunch zipped into the front pocket.
Omari had been quiet in the car park before the game.
He had retied his laces twice and asked Kenji, for the third time, whether his shirt was on the right way round.
“Dad finishes work at five,” he said, frowning at his phone.
“He reckons he might make the second half.
He’s been stuck at work for nearly every game this season, though.”
Then he folded his jacket, laid it on the end seat of the front row, and asked the woman beside it if she would mind keeping it free.
At half time the coach crouched in front of the bench.
“Every time one of you touches the ball, you look over here,” she said, tapping her clipboard.
“I’m not on the court.”
Kenji felt his face go hot.
Beside him, Omari stared at his shoes and said nothing.
The second half was faster.
Omari hit two shots from the corner, the way he nearly always did.
Kenji missed his first shot from the top of the arc, then made the next one from exactly the same spot.
Every few minutes Omari glanced past the bench at the end seat of the front row, where his jacket was still lying flat.
With a minute left the score was tied at 41 all.
The far door opened, and a man in an orange work vest came in and stopped just inside it.
He did not go to the seat with the jacket.
He stood with his arms folded, as if sitting down might make him miss something.
Omari had his back to the door and did not see him.
Ten seconds to go.
Kenji’s defender lunged for the ball and missed, and suddenly Kenji was alone at the top of the arc.
Nobody was within two metres of him.
He knew it, and from the roar in the stands, so did everyone else.
He looked once at the door.
Then he turned and fired a hard pass into the corner, where Omari caught it, rose and let it go.
The buzzer sounded with the ball still in the air.
It dropped through the net.
Omari spun round with both fists up, and then he saw the door.
For a second he just stood there.
Then he was running, and his dad was laughing and holding out his arms, and the orange vest disappeared under a crowd of players.
When the stadium had nearly emptied, the coach stopped Kenji on his way to the bench.
“You were open at the top,” she said.
“Wide open.”
She looked at him for a long moment, then across at Omari and his dad, who were still standing by the door.
She nodded slowly and wrote something on her clipboard.
“The list goes up on Monday,” she said, and walked off.
His mum was waiting in the car park with the engine running.
She didn’t ask about the squad.
She asked if he wanted to stop for dumplings on the way home, and when they pulled into the driveway, she nodded up at the hoop above the garage.
“Same time tomorrow?” she said.
Kenji grinned.
“Same time.”

passages.title: Toad's Adventures
passages.source: From The Wind in the Willows by Kenneth Grahame (1908), Chapter VIII, abridged
paras: She was particularly fond of animals, and, besides her canary, whose cage hung on a nail in the massive wall of the keep by day, to the great annoyance of prisoners who relished an after-dinner nap, and was shrouded in an antimacassar on the parlour table at night, she kept several piebald mice and a restless revolving squirrel.
This kind-hearted girl, pitying the misery of Toad, said to her father one day, 'Father!
I can't bear to see that poor beast so unhappy, and getting so thin!
You let me have the managing of him.
You know how fond of animals I am.
I'll make him eat from my hand, and sit up, and do all sorts of things.'
Her father replied that she could do what she liked with him.
He was tired of Toad, and his sulks and his airs and his meanness.
So that day she went on her errand of mercy, and knocked at the door of Toad's cell.
'Now, cheer up, Toad,' she said, coaxingly, on entering, 'and sit up and dry your eyes and be a sensible animal.
And do try and eat a bit of dinner.
See, I've brought you some of mine, hot from the oven!'
It was bubble-and-squeak, between two plates, and its fragrance filled the narrow cell.

The penetrating smell of cabbage reached the nose of Toad as he lay prostrate in his misery on the floor, and gave him the idea for a moment that perhaps life was not such a blank and desperate thing as he had imagined.
But still he wailed, and kicked with his legs, and refused to be comforted.

So the wise girl retired for the time, but, of course, a good deal of the smell of hot cabbage remained behind, as it will do, and Toad, between his sobs, sniffed and reflected, and gradually began to think new and inspiring thoughts: of chivalry, and poetry, and deeds still to be done; of broad meadows, and cattle browsing in them, raked by sun and wind; of kitchen-gardens, and straight herb-borders, and warm snap-dragon beset by bees; and of the comforting clink of dishes set down on the table at Toad Hall, and the scrape of chair-legs on the floor as every one pulled himself close up to his work.

When the girl returned, some hours later, she carried a tray, with a cup of fragrant tea steaming on it; and a plate piled up with very hot buttered toast, cut thick, very brown on both sides, with the butter running through the holes in it in great golden drops, like honey from the honeycomb.

The smell of that buttered toast simply talked to Toad, and with no uncertain voice; talked of warm kitchens, of breakfasts on bright frosty mornings, of cosy parlour firesides on winter evenings, when one's ramble was over and slippered feet were propped on the fender; of the purring of contented cats, and the twitter of sleepy canaries.

Toad sat up on end once more, dried his eyes, sipped his tea and munched his toast, and soon began talking freely about himself, and the house he lived in, and his doings there, and how important he was, and what a lot his friends thought of him.
The gaoler's daughter saw that the topic was doing him as much good as the tea, as indeed it was, and encouraged him to go on.

passages.title: The Garage Light
paras: The winter I was eleven, my cousin Mateo came to stay with us for a term while his parents finished packing up their house in Darwin.
He was thirteen, so he got my room.
I got the fold out couch in the study, which squeaked whenever I rolled over and smelt faintly of Dad’s printer ink.
Mum said it was only ten weeks.
I said ten weeks was most of my life, which even then I knew was not true.
Mateo hardly spoke.
At dinner he ate quickly, said, “Thanks, Aunty,” and went back to my room.
I decided he thought our house was boring.
When Mum made her lasagne, the one my friends asked for at every birthday, he left a corner of it on the side of his plate, and I took that as proof that he thought our food was worse than boring.
Every night at eight o’clock he phoned home.
The study shared a wall with my old room, and the wall was thin.
I couldn’t make out much, only his voice going up at the ends of questions, and once, very clearly, “Is Pepper eating?”
Pepper was their old cattle dog.
I didn’t wonder why anyone would ask about a dog’s dinner every single night.
In the third week he started going into the garage after school.
He stayed there until dinner, and when he came in, his hands were black to the wrists.
Dad’s toolbox, which nobody was allowed to touch, had moved from the shelf to the bench.
Through the laundry door I heard clanking, then a long silence, then more clanking.
I told my sister Nadia that Mateo was wrecking Dad’s tools because he was angry about being sent to stay with us.
Nadia was fifteen and knew everything.
“Or he’s bored,” she said.
“Have you asked him?”
I had not asked him.
I had no intention of asking him.
Instead I kept a list in the back of my maths book.
Lasagne left on plate.
Toolbox moved.
Door to my room always shut.
Did not laugh at Dad’s joke about the possums.
I was going to show it to Mum when it had ten things on it.
I got as far as seven.
On the last Saturday of the term, Dad called me out to the driveway.
My old bike was leaning against the letterbox.
Nobody had ridden it since the chain snapped and the back wheel buckled the summer before, and I had told everyone, loudly and often, that I had outgrown it anyway.
Now the wheel spun straight, the chain was new and black, and the seat had been raised as high as it would go.
Someone had wound green tape around the handlebars, the way the older riders did at the skate park.
“He asked me on the first night whether you had a bike,” Dad said.
“He’s been at it every afternoon.
He wanted it done before he left.”
Mateo was standing in the garage doorway with his hands in his pockets, looking at the bike rather than at me.
“The seat goes higher if you need it,” he said.
It was the most words he had said to me in ten weeks.
I rode to the end of the street and back while he watched.
I did not show anyone the list.
That night I tore it into very small pieces and pushed them to the bottom of the study bin, under the printer paper, where I was fairly sure nobody would look.
Mum told me, much later, that Mateo had made her promise not to say a word about the bike, even when she heard me complaining about the noise.
It was years before I understood the phone calls.
At a wedding, when we were both grown up, Mateo told me that Pepper had stopped eating the week he left Darwin, and that the bike was the only thing that had stopped him worrying about her.
She was fine by the time he got home, he said, and as greedy as ever.
By then I was a grown woman, old enough to be embarrassed about the list, and to wonder how many other lists I had kept about people I had never asked.

passages.title: Inside the Grid
paras: Every morning, thousands of Australians fold the newspaper back to the puzzle page, or open it on a phone, and start filling in squares.
Few of them stop to think that someone made that puzzle, usually weeks before, and that it may have taken that person far longer to build than any solver will spend on it.
Crossword makers are known as setters, and most of them work alone.
The crossword is younger than many people think.
The first one was printed in a New York newspaper in December 1913, in a holiday puzzle section, and it was shaped like a diamond rather than a square.
Its setter was a journalist named Arthur Wynne.
Within about ten years the puzzles had become a craze in America, and by the 1930s they were appearing in newspapers across Britain.
Most setters begin with the grid, not the clues.
The black squares are usually arranged so that the pattern looks exactly the same when the grid is turned upside down.
Nothing about solving the puzzle needs this, and a few setters ignore it, but most keep it because solvers expect a tidy grid, and a lopsided one looks careless.
Next comes a choice that decides how hard the puzzle will feel.

In most American style grids, every letter is checked: each white square sits in an across answer and a down answer at the same time, so a solver who is stuck on one clue can borrow letters from the other.
The cryptic crosswords printed in Britain and Australia usually check only about half of the letters in each answer.
A solver who cannot crack a clue there may get no help at all with some of its squares.
Then the setter fills the grid with words, which can take an hour or a whole afternoon, and only then writes the clues.
In a cryptic crossword, each clue is a small trick in two parts.
One part is a plain definition of the answer, and it usually sits at the very start or the very end of the clue.
The rest is wordplay: a second route to the same answer, built from hidden words, sounds or letters rearranged.
Setters also borrow words that can mean something unexpected.
In a cryptic clue, a “flower” is often not a rose or a daisy at all, but the Thames or the Nile, because a river is something that flows.
Before a puzzle reaches the paper, at least one test solver works through it.
Their job is to check for mistakes, but also for clues that are unfair: a clue with two possible answers, or one that only makes sense inside the setter’s head.
A setter can be sure that a clue is clever and still discover that the test solver read it a completely different way.
Many setters say that the most useful thing a test solver can write is a single question mark beside a clue.
What makes a clue fair?
Setters often answer with one rule: the solver must be able to reach the answer from the words in the clue alone, without having to read the setter’s mind.
A good clue can be hard, and it can mislead on purpose, but once the answer arrives, every word in the clue should make sense.
That is why many setters say the best reaction to a clue is not a cheer but a groan.
A groan means the solver was fooled fairly.
The answer was there all along, in plain sight, and the solver walked straight past it.
It is a strange job, spending days on something that is meant to be finished over breakfast and then thrown away.
But for a setter, there is no better compliment than that groan.

passages.title: Andy’s Gone With Cattle
paras: Our Andy's gone to battle now
'Gainst Drought, the red marauder;
Our Andy's gone with cattle now
Across the Queensland border.
He's left us in dejection now;
Our hearts with him are roving.
It's dull on this selection now,
Since Andy went a-droving.
Who now shall wear the cheerful face
In times when things are slackest?
And who shall whistle round the place
When Fortune frowns her blackest?
Oh, who shall cheek the squatter now
When he comes round us snarling?
His tongue is growing hotter now
Since Andy cross'd the Darling.
The gates are out of order now,
In storms the 'riders' rattle;
For far across the border now
Our Andy's gone with cattle.
Poor Aunty's looking thin and white;
And Uncle's cross with worry;
And poor old Blucher howls all night
Since Andy left Macquarie.
Oh, may the showers in torrents fall,
And all the tanks run over;
And may the grass grow green and tall
In pathways of the drover;
And may good angels send the rain
On desert stretches sandy;
And when the summer comes again
God grant 'twill bring us Andy.

rounds.cue: The speaker prays for rain.
The water tanks overflowing.
Fence rails rattle in storms.
Andy has gone over into Queensland.
dejection
